claim: Plasmodium falciparum actin is implicated in endocytosis, cytokinesis and inheritance of the chloroplast-like organelle called the apicoplast.
source: In addition to its role in erythrocyte invasion, Plasmodium falciparum actin is implicated in endocytosis, cytokinesis and inheritance of the chloroplast-like organelle called the apicoplast.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of P. falciparum actin, supported by prior research.

claim: The inability to visualise filamentous actin (F-actin) dynamics had restricted the characterisation of both F-actin and actin regulatory proteins in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Previously, the inability to visualise filamentous actin (F-actin) dynamics had restricted the characterisation of both F-actin and actin regulatory proteins, a limitation we recently overcame for Toxoplasma (Periz et al, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Periz et al, 2017) that overcame this limitation in Toxoplasma.

claim: Actin-binding chromobodies can be expressed and validated as F-actin-sensors in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Here, we have expressed and validated actin-binding chromobodies as F-actin-sensors in Plasmodium falciparum and characterised in-vivo actin dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: F-actin in Plasmodium falciparum can be chemically modulated.
source: F-actin could be chemically modulated, and genetically disrupted upon conditionally deleting actin-1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of cytochalasin-D and jasplakinolide treatment.

claim: F-actin in Plasmodium falciparum can be genetically disrupted upon conditionally deleting actin-1.
source: F-actin could be chemically modulated, and genetically disrupted upon conditionally deleting actin-1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using conditional knockout of actin-1.

claim: Formin-2 is responsible for apicoplast inheritance in both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
source: In a comparative approach, we demonstrate that Formin-2, a predicted nucleator of F-actin, is responsible for apicoplast inheritance in both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma, and additionally mediates efficient cytokinesis in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from conditional mutants in both organisms.

claim: Formin-2 mediates efficient cytokinesis in Plasmodium.
source: In a comparative approach, we demonstrate that Formin-2, a predicted nucleator of F-actin, is responsible for apicoplast inheritance in both Plasmodium and Toxoplasma, and additionally mediates efficient cytokinesis in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing cytokinesis defects in Formin-2 knockout parasites.

claim: Formin-2 is the primary F-actin nucleator during apicomplexan intracellular growth.
source: Together, our data indicate that Formin-2 is the primary F-actin nucleator during apicomplexan intracellular growth, mediating multiple essential functions.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by experimental data showing loss of F-actin dynamics upon Formin-2 disruption.

claim: Malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum causes approximately 500,000 deaths annually.
source: One of its notorious members, the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, is a major health concern in developing nations, causing ~500,000 deaths annually (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii infects almost a third of the global human population.
source: Another member, Toxoplasma gondii is a highly successful parasite infecting almost a third of the global human population and can be fatal in immunocompromised patients (Torgerson and Mastroiacovo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torgerson and Mastroiacovo, 2013.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii can be fatal in immunocompromised patients.
source: Another member, Toxoplasma gondii is a highly successful parasite infecting almost a third of the global human population and can be fatal in immunocompromised patients (Torgerson and Mastroiacovo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torgerson and Mastroiacovo, 2013.

claim: Actins encoded by apicomplexan parasites are highly divergent compared to canonical actins from other eukaryotes.
source: Actins encoded by apicomplexan parasites are highly divergent compared to canonical actins from other eukaryotes (Douglas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Douglas et al., 2018.

claim: Apicomplexan actins form only short, unstable polymers in vitro due to different polymerisation kinetics.
source: In-vitro, apicomplexan actins form only short, unstable polymers due to different polymerisation kinetics, caused by variation of certain key amino acids otherwise conserved in metazoans (Kumpula and Kursula, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumpula and Kursula, 2015.

claim: Different polymerisation kinetics of apicomplexan actins are caused by variation of certain key amino acids otherwise conserved in metazoans.
source: In-vitro, apicomplexan actins form only short, unstable polymers due to different polymerisation kinetics, caused by variation of certain key amino acids otherwise conserved in metazoans (Kumpula and Kursula, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumpula and Kursula, 2015.

claim: F-actin binding chromobodies were successfully expressed in T. gondii.
source: In a recent study, it was shown that actin-binding nanobodies fused to epitope tags could be expressed in Toxoplasma gondii, allowing for the first time to analyse F-actin localisation and dynamics in living parasites (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Actin-binding chromobodies allowed for the first time to analyse F-actin localisation and dynamics in living Toxoplasma gondii parasites.
source: In a recent study, it was shown that actin-binding nanobodies fused to epitope tags could be expressed in Toxoplasma gondii, allowing for the first time to analyse F-actin localisation and dynamics in living parasites (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Actin-binding chromobodies bind to P. falciparum actin in vitro.
source: Another recent study showed that these nanobodies also bind to P. falciparum actin in-vitro (Bookwalter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bookwalter et al., 2017.

claim: F-actin in T. gondii can form an extensive intra-vacuolar network that appears to be involved in material exchange and synchronisation of parasite division.
source: Intriguingly, in this parasite, F-actin can form an extensive intra-vacuolar network that appears to be involved in material exchange and synchronisation of parasite division (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: F-actin is believed to provide the force for host cell invasion and gliding motility in apicomplexans.
source: Until recently, studies on apicomplexan F-actin focused on its critical role during host cell invasion and gliding motility (Soldati et al., 2004; Baum et al., 2008a), where it is believed to provide the force for both processes (Frénal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soldati et al., 2004; Baum et al., 2008a; and Frénal et al., 2017.

claim: Conditional mutants for actin-1 in P. falciparum and T. gondii highlight critical roles of F-actin during intracellular parasite development.
source: However, recent studies using conditional mutants for actin-1 in two apicomplexans, P. falciparum and T. gondii highlight additional critical roles of F-actin during intracellular parasite development (Das et al., 2017; Periz et al., 2017; Whitelaw et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Das et al., 2017; Periz et al., 2017; Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Inheritance of the apicoplast is a conserved function of F-actin in apicomplexans.
source: Intriguingly, some functions, such as inheritance of the chloroplast-like organelle, the apicoplast, appear to be conserved (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Das et al., 2017; Whitelaw et al., 2017), while differences for the dependency of F-actin can be observed for other critical steps of the asexual life cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Das et al., 2017; Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Host cell invasion is possible without actin-1 in T. gondii, albeit at highly reduced levels.
source: For example, host cell invasion is possible without actin-1 (albeit at highly reduced levels) in case of T. gondii (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Whitelaw et al., 2017), while it is completely blocked in case of P. falciparum (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claim: Host cell invasion is completely blocked without actin-1 in P. falciparum.
source: For example, host cell invasion is possible without actin-1 (albeit at highly reduced levels) in case of T. gondii (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Egarter et al., 2014; Whitelaw et al., 2017), while it is completely blocked in case of P. falciparum (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: P. falciparum does not require actin dynamics for egress from the host cell.
source: In contrast, P. falciparum does not require actin dynamics for egress from the host cell (Das et al., 2017; Perrin et al., 2018), while it is essential for T. gondii.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Das et al., 2017; Perrin et al., 2018.

claim: Actin dynamics are essential for egress from the host cell in T. gondii.
source: In contrast, P. falciparum does not require actin dynamics for egress from the host cell (Das et al., 2017; Perrin et al., 2018), while it is essential for T. gondii.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between the two parasites, implied from prior research.

claim: Completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum is dependent on actin dynamics.
source: Additionally, completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum is dependent on actin dynamics (Das et al., 2017), while no such dependency has been noted for T. gondii.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: No dependency on actin dynamics for cytokinesis has been noted for T. gondii.
source: Additionally, completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum is dependent on actin dynamics (Das et al., 2017), while no such dependency has been noted for T. gondii.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior research.

claim: CB-EME labels actin filaments throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle of P. falciparum.
source: CB-EME labels actin filaments throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle with, in ring stages (0–8 hr), trophozoite stages (20 hr) and in 44 hr schizont stages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: F-actin structures labeled by CB-EME disappear upon cytochalasin-D treatment in P. falciparum.
source: White arrows mark structures, in all likelihood F-actin, which disappear upon cytochalasin-D treatment (+CytoD), and islands of F-actin are stabilised upon jasplakinolide treatment (+JAS).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Islands of F-actin are stabilised upon jasplakinolide treatment in P. falciparum.
source: White arrows mark structures, in all likelihood F-actin, which disappear upon cytochalasin-D treatment (+CytoD), and islands of F-actin are stabilised upon jasplakinolide treatment (+JAS).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A bright fluorescent signal of F-actin appears at a polar end of the merozoite immediately after host cell rupture in 56 ± 9% of egressed merozoites.
source: Time lapse imaging of schizonts undergoing egress from the host cell, reveals a bright fluorescent signal (CB-EME) of F-actin (white arrows) at a polar end of the merozoite, appearing immediately after host cell rupture (occurs in 56 ± 9% egressed merozoites, N = 260 from three independent experiments).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cytochalasin-D treatment completely prevents the polar polymerisation of F-actin in all egressed merozoites.
source: Cytochalasin-D treatment completely prevents the polar polymerisation of F-actin in all cells (+CytoD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: F-actin polymerises at the apical end of invading merozoites prior to invasion.
source: IFA of invading merozoites with the junction marker RON4 shows CB-EME staining close to the RON4 stain, implying that F-actin polymerises at the apical end prior to invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The F-actin network and dynamics can be visualised in P. falciparum gametocytes.
source: The F-actin network and dynamics can be visualised in gametocytes (see also Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CB-HALO expressing parasites show staining with anti-PfACT1 and with an anti-HALO antibody.
source: IFA of CB-HALO expressing parasites showing staining with anti-PfACT1 and with an anti-HALO antibody.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Filamentous structures labeled by CB-HALO in DMSO controls are lost upon cytochalasin-D-treatment.
source: Imaging of CB-HALO by addition of the ligand TMR: Left panels: Filamentous structures in DMSO controls (white arrows) are lost upon cytochalasin-D-treatment (+CytoD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Intensity of CB-HALO expression and filament structures are lost upon PfACT1 disruption.
source: Right panels: Intensity of CB-HALO expression and filament structures (red) are lost upon PfACT1 disruption (RAP, PfAct1 cKO).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: High intensity of CB-HALO (F-actin) is observed around the FV or at the basal end of newly forming daughter cells in DMSO parasites.
source: IFA with anti-GAP45 antibodies show high intensity of CB-HALO (therefore F-actin) around the FV (or at the basal end of newly forming daughter cells) in DMSO parasites, which is lost upon excision of pfact1 (RAP, PfAct1 cKO).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: High intensity of CB-HALO around the FV is lost upon excision of pfact1.
source: IFA with anti-GAP45 antibodies show high intensity of CB-HALO (therefore F-actin) around the FV (or at the basal end of newly forming daughter cells) in DMSO parasites, which is lost upon excision of pfact1 (RAP, PfAct1 cKO).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Deconvoluted time lapse images show rapid changes in peripheral F-actin accumulations in the order of seconds.
source: Deconvoluted time lapse images show rapid changes (in the order of seconds) in peripheral F-actin accumulations (white arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: F-actin-rich protrusions at the periphery of the parasite cell body are visible in 45 ± 12 % of cells by standard fluorescence microscopy.
source: F-actin-rich protrusions at the periphery of the parasite cell body (white arrows) could be seen by standard fluorescence microscopy in 45 ± 12 % cells (N = 195 from three independent experiments), which could be disrupted by cytochalasin-D (+CytoD) and jasplakinolide (+JAS).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: F-actin-rich protrusions at the periphery of the parasite cell body can be disrupted by cytochalasin-D and jasplakinolide.
source: F-actin-rich protrusions at the periphery of the parasite cell body (white arrows) could be seen by standard fluorescence microscopy in 45 ± 12 % cells (N = 195 from three independent experiments), which could be disrupted by cytochalasin-D (+CytoD) and jasplakinolide (+JAS).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Only actin-1 (pfact1) is expressed in all life-cycle stages of P. falciparum.
source: Of the two actin genes present in P. falciparum (Gardner et al., 2002), only actin-1 (pfact1, GeneID: PF3D7_1246200) is expressed in all life-cycle stages and is the only actin expressed during asexual replicative stages, whereas actin-2 (GeneID: PF3D7_1412500) expression is confined to the sexual gametocyte and insect stages (Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2002; Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014.

claim: Actin-1 is the only actin expressed during asexual replicative stages of P. falciparum.
source: Of the two actin genes present in P. falciparum (Gardner et al., 2002), only actin-1 (pfact1, GeneID: PF3D7_1246200) is expressed in all life-cycle stages and is the only actin expressed during asexual replicative stages, whereas actin-2 (GeneID: PF3D7_1412500) expression is confined to the sexual gametocyte and insect stages (Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014.

claim: Actin-2 expression in P. falciparum is confined to the sexual gametocyte and insect stages.
source: Of the two actin genes present in P. falciparum (Gardner et al., 2002), only actin-1 (pfact1, GeneID: PF3D7_1246200) is expressed in all life-cycle stages and is the only actin expressed during asexual replicative stages, whereas actin-2 (GeneID: PF3D7_1412500) expression is confined to the sexual gametocyte and insect stages (Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deligianni et al., 2011; Vahokoski et al., 2014.

claim: P. falciparum undergoes a 48 hr asexual replicative cycle in the intermediate human host.
source: P. falciparum undergoes a 48 hr asexual replicative cycle in the intermediate human host where it invades into, grows and replicates within erythrocytes, causing all clinical manifestations of the disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: P. falciparum invades into, grows and replicates within erythrocytes, causing all clinical manifestations of the disease.
source: P. falciparum undergoes a 48 hr asexual replicative cycle in the intermediate human host where it invades into, grows and replicates within erythrocytes, causing all clinical manifestations of the disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: After invasion, the P. falciparum merozoite loses its ovoid shape to become amoeboid.
source: After invasion, the merozoite form of the parasite (similar to T. gondii tachyzoites) establishes itself within a parasitophorous vacuole (PV), loses its ovoid shape to become amoeboid and feeds on host haemoglobin creating a food vacuole (FV) where haem is detoxified (Grüring et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grüring et al., 2011.

claim: P. falciparum feeds on host haemoglobin creating a food vacuole (FV) where haem is detoxified.
source: After invasion, the merozoite form of the parasite (similar to T. gondii tachyzoites) establishes itself within a parasitophorous vacuole (PV), loses its ovoid shape to become amoeboid and feeds on host haemoglobin creating a food vacuole (FV) where haem is detoxified (Grüring et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grüring et al., 2011.

claim: Actin has been implicated in transport/fusion of haemoglobin-filled vesicles in P. falciparum.
source: Interestingly, actin has been implicated in transport/fusion of haemoglobin-filled vesicles (Elliott et al., 2008; Smythe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2008; Smythe et al., 2008.

claim: P. falciparum replicates by a process best described as internal budding, where daughter parasites develop within the mother.
source: The parasite then replicates by a process best described as internal budding, where daughter parasites develop within the mother (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Francia and Striepen, 2014.

claim: T. gondii forms only two daughters at a time in a process called endodyogeny.
source: In the case of T. gondii, only two daughters are formed at a time in a process called endodyogeny.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. gondii biology.

claim: Malaria parasite replication within the erythrocyte, termed schizogony, results in the formation of 16–32 merozoites at once.
source: In contrast, malaria parasite replication within the erythrocyte, termed schizogony, results in the formation of 16–32 merozoites at once.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: Towards the end of a replicative cycle, P. falciparum forms its invasion-related organelles de novo: the inner membrane complex (IMC), micronemes and rhoptries.
source: Towards the end of a replicative cycle the parasite forms its invasion-related organelles de novo: the inner membrane complex (IMC), micronemes and rhoptries.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: Parasite mitochondria and the apicoplast undergo growth and division and are trafficked into each daughter cell in P. falciparum.
source: In contrast, parasite mitochondria and the apicoplast undergo growth and division and are trafficked into each daughter cell (Bannister et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bannister et al., 2000.

claim: Endodyogeny and schizogony are believed to use a conserved molecular machinery.
source: Although endodyogeny and schizogony appear different, it is believed that both processes use a conserved molecular machinery. Indeed, independent studies identified the same factors to be critical for both replicative modes (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Francia and Striepen, 2014.

claim: Independent studies identified the same factors to be critical for both endodyogeny and schizogony.
source: Although endodyogeny and schizogony appear different, it is believed that both processes use a conserved molecular machinery. Indeed, independent studies identified the same factors to be critical for both replicative modes (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Francia and Striepen, 2014.

claim: Inheritance of the apicoplast is compromised during schizogony in PfACT1 conditional mutants.
source: We recently characterised a conditional mutant of PfACT1 and observed that in good agreement with the function of actin in T. gondii (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), inheritance of the apicoplast is compromised during schizogony (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013; Das et al., 2017.

claim: Common actin-labelling probes such as Phalloidin do not label apicomplexan actin.
source: Common actin-labelling probes such as Phalloidin do not label apicomplexan actin and LifeAct could not be successfully expressed in these parasites (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: LifeAct could not be successfully expressed in apicomplexan parasites.
source: Common actin-labelling probes such as Phalloidin do not label apicomplexan actin and LifeAct could not be successfully expressed in these parasites (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Actin-binding chromobodies were successfully expressed in T. gondii and shown to have minimal effect on actin dynamics.
source: Recently, actin-binding single-domain nanobodies tagged to fluorescent probes, called actin-chromobodies, were successfully expressed in T. gondii and shown to have minimal effect on actin dynamics (Periz et al., 2017), as also demonstrated in other eukaryotic cells (Rocchetti et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015; Melak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Periz et al., 2017; Rocchetti et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015; Melak et al., 2017.

claim: Actin-chromobodies have minimal effect on actin dynamics in other eukaryotic cells.
source: Recently, actin-binding single-domain nanobodies tagged to fluorescent probes, called actin-chromobodies, were successfully expressed in T. gondii and shown to have minimal effect on actin dynamics (Periz et al., 2017), as also demonstrated in other eukaryotic cells (Rocchetti et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015; Melak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rocchetti et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015; Melak et al., 2017.

claim: Actin-chromobodies could faithfully label purified Plasmodium actin in in-vitro experiments.
source: Furthermore, these chromobodies could faithfully label purified Plasmodium actin in in-vitro experiments (Bookwalter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bookwalter et al., 2017.

claim: F-actin is found in proximity to the apicoplast throughout intracellular growth in P. falciparum.
source: Interestingly, we find F-actin in proximity to the apicoplast throughout intracellular growth, leading to the question of which actin regulatory proteins are involved in this process.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Most actin nucleation proteins such as the Arp2/3 complex and the WAVE/WASP complex are missing in apicomplexans.
source: Most actin nucleation proteins such as the Arp2/3 complex and the WAVE/WASP complex, and actin cross-linkers such as α-actinin and fimbrin are missing in apicomplexans (Baum et al., 2006; Schüler and Matuschewski, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2006; Schüler and Matuschewski, 2006.

claim: Actin cross-linkers such as α-actinin and fimbrin are missing in apicomplexans.
source: Most actin nucleation proteins such as the Arp2/3 complex and the WAVE/WASP complex, and actin cross-linkers such as α-actinin and fimbrin are missing in apicomplexans (Baum et al., 2006; Schüler and Matuschewski, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baum et al., 2006; Schüler and Matuschewski, 2006.

claim: Two conserved nucleators found in P. falciparum are the formins, Formin-1 (PfFRM1) and Formin-2 (PfFRM2).
source: Two conserved nucleators found in P. falciparum are the formins, Formin-1 (PfFRM1) and Formin-2 (PfFRM2) which localise to distinct compartments in the cell (Baum et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: PfFRM1 and PfFRM2 localise to distinct compartments in the cell.
source: Two conserved nucleators found in P. falciparum are the formins, Formin-1 (PfFRM1) and Formin-2 (PfFRM2) which localise to distinct compartments in the cell (Baum et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: Orthologs of both formins have been implicated in host cell invasion in T. gondii.
source: Orthologs of both formins have been implicated in host cell invasion in T. gondii (Daher et al., 2010), with T. gondii Formin-2 (TgFRM2) also being implicated in apicoplast maintenance (Jacot et al., 2013) – leading to inconsistencies in reports and questions whether the two formins have conserved or divergent functions in both parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daher et al., 2010.

claim: T. gondii Formin-2 (TgFRM2) has been implicated in apicoplast maintenance.
source: Orthologs of both formins have been implicated in host cell invasion in T. gondii (Daher et al., 2010), with T. gondii Formin-2 (TgFRM2) also being implicated in apicoplast maintenance (Jacot et al., 2013) – leading to inconsistencies in reports and questions whether the two formins have conserved or divergent functions in both parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jacot et al., 2013.

claim: A recent study suggested distinct, non-overlapping functions for the three formins in T. gondii.
source: Indeed, a recent study, using the F-actin chromobody as described previously (Periz et al., 2017), suggested distinct, non-overlapping functions for the three formins in T. gondii (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Periz et al., 2017; Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Formin-2 localises in close proximity to apicoplasts in both P. falciparum and T. gondii.
source: Here we performed a careful comparison of the role of Formin-2 in P. falciparum and T. gondii and demonstrate that it localises in close proximity to apicoplasts in both parasites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum.
source: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 not only results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum and a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii, it also leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both genera.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 results in a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii.
source: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 not only results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum and a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii, it also leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both genera.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both P. falciparum and T. gondii.
source: Conditional disruption of Formin-2 not only results in a complete abrogation of actin dynamics in P. falciparum and a loss of an intracellular F-actin polymerisation centre in T. gondii, it also leads to defects in apicoplast inheritance in both genera.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Formin-2 is additionally involved in completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum, in contrast to Toxoplasma.
source: In contrast to Toxoplasma, Formin-2 is additionally involved in completion of cytokinesis in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Actin-chromobodies were expressed under control of the heat shock protein 86 (hsp86) promoter to obtain expression throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle.
source: Actin-chromobodies (Chromotek) were expressed under control of the heat shock protein 86 (hsp86) promoter (Crabb and Cowman, 1996) to obtain expression throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle.
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation to Crabb and Cowman, 1996.

claim: Parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged with emerald or halo tags were successfully generated.
source: We succeeded in generating parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged either with the emerald tag (CB-EME) (Figure 1B), or the halo tag (CB-HALO) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the expression of these constructs does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum as previously reported for Toxoplasma (Periz et al., 2017) and other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Expression of actin-chromobodies does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum.
source: We succeeded in generating parasites stably expressing actin-chromobodies tagged either with the emerald tag (CB-EME) (Figure 1B), or the halo tag (CB-HALO) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the expression of these constructs does not have a major deleterious impact on the fitness of P. falciparum as previously reported for Toxoplasma (Periz et al., 2017) and other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is inferred from successful generation of stable parasites and supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Dynamic filamentous structures were evident in both CB-EME and CB-HALO expressing parasites throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle and in gametocytes.
source: Dynamic filamentous structures were evident in both CB-EME (Figure 1) and CB-HALO expressing parasites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) throughout the 48 hr asexual life cycle (see also Videos 1, 2, 3 and 4) and in gametocytes (Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Filamentous structures labeled by chromobodies could be completely disrupted by treatment with cytochalasin-D.
source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claim: Filamentous structures labeled by chromobodies could be stabilised by addition of Jasplakinolide.
source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 3.

claim: Chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
source: These structures could be completely disrupted by treatment with F-actin destabilising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) or stabilised by addition of the depolymerisation inhibitor Jasplakinolide (JAS) (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) (Figure 1C bottom panels and Video 3), demonstrating that chromobodies bind F-actin structures in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of F-actin modulating drugs on chromobody-labeled structures.

claim: Expression of CB-EME resulted in a better signal-to-noise ratio than CB-HALO.
source: However, while both chromobody versions labelled similar structures, we found that expression of CB-EME resulted in a better signal-to-noise ratio. This is probably because no permeable, fluorescent ligand needs to be added for visualisation.
evidence: This is an observation from the study with a speculative explanation.

claim: Some F-actin structures were highly dynamic, changing within time-scales of seconds, while other structures appeared stable over tens of seconds.
source: Some F-actin structures were highly dynamic, changing within a time-scales of seconds, while other structures appeared stable over tens of seconds (Video 3, see also quantifications below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in videos and quantifications.

claim: F-actin rich islands at the periphery of ~60% of ring and early trophozoite stage parasites were observed.
source: On observing chromobody-expressing parasites during ring and early trophozoite stages we noted F-actin rich islands at the periphery of ~60% parasites (n = 50) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2.

claim: Peripheral F-actin accumulations were highly dynamic, changing in order of seconds.
source: These F-actin accumulations were highly dynamic, changing in order of seconds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2.

claim: Upon treatment with cytochalasin-D, the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared.
source: Upon treatment with the F-actin depolymerising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration of 1 µM) the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), while the multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted (Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Video 6.

claim: The multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted by cytochalasin-D treatment.
source: Upon treatment with the F-actin depolymerising drug cytochalasin-D (30 min, final concentration of 1 µM) the peripheral, highly dynamic accumulations completely disappeared (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), while the multi-lobed structures of the parasite were not disrupted (Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 6.

claim: Jasplakinolide disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments.
source: The F-actin stabilising drug jasplakinolide also disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), implying the requirement of dynamic regulation of F-actin for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Dynamic regulation of F-actin is required for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
source: The F-actin stabilising drug jasplakinolide also disrupted peripheral F-actin and resulted in formation of stable thick filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B lower panel), implying the requirement of dynamic regulation of F-actin for peripheral F-actin accumulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of jasplakinolide on peripheral F-actin.

claim: Compound-1 and -2 are reversible inhibitors of protein kinase G that stall schizont development at very mature stages without allowing egress.
source: Reversible inhibitors of protein kinase G, Compound-1 and −2, stall schizont development at very mature stages without allowing them to undergo egress (Collins et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2013b.

claim: Upon washing away Compound-2, parasites egressed normally with the concomitant appearance of F-actin accumulation at the apical tip of the parasite.
source: Upon washing away Compound-2, the parasites egressed normally with the concomitant appearance of F-actin accumulation at the apical tip of the parasite (Figure 1D, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Video 4.

claim: Cytochalasin-D treatment allowed normal egress of parasites but completely abrogated F-actin polymerisation at the apical tip following egress.
source: Cytochalasin-D treatment (30 min, final concentration 1 µM) allowed normal egress of parasites, as previously observed (Weiss et al., 2015), but completely abrogated F-actin polymerisation at the apical tip following egress (Figure 1D,+CytoD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citation to Weiss et al., 2015.

claim: F-actin accumulates just behind the RON4 ring in invading merozoites.
source: Furthermore, we performed IFA on invading merozoites using rhoptry neck protein 4 (RON4) as a junctional marker. We verified that F-actin accumulates just behind the RON4 ring (Figure 1E) confirming previous observations made with an antibody preferentially recognising F-actin in P. falciparum (Riglar et al., 2011; Angrisano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Riglar et al., 2011; Angrisano et al., 2012.

claim: Gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2.
source: In contrast to asexual parasites, gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2, and exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips (Hliscs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claim: Gametocytes exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips.
source: In contrast to asexual parasites, gametocytes express both PfACT1 and actin-2, and exhibit F-actin staining along the length of the parasite and at the tips (Hliscs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claim: CB-EME expression in gametocytes showed intense dynamic F-actin structures at their tips and running along the whole body of the cell.
source: Upon expression of CB-EME, gametocytes showed intense dynamic F-actin structures at their tips and running along the whole body of the cell (Figure 1F and Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Video 5.

claim: The dynamic F-actin network in gametocytes appears very similar to the one reported by Hliscs et al. (2015), which lies beneath the IMC of the gametocyte.
source: Importantly, this dynamic network appears very similar to the one reported by Hliscs et al. (2015), which has been shown to lie beneath the IMC of the gametocyte.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to prior work cited (Hliscs et al., 2015).

claim: Actin-chromobodies do not distinguish between PfACT1 and actin-2.
source: It is important to note that actin-chromobodies do not distinguish between PfACT1 and actin-2 and therefore the observed filaments could potentially be composed of both proteins.
evidence: This is a limitation of the chromobody technology stated by the authors.

claim: During the gametocyte stage, F-actin forms a dynamic and extensive network that passes through the whole cell and is enriched at the tips of the parasite.
source: We therefore confirm previous data obtained with antibodies directed against F-actin (Hliscs et al., 2015) and show that during the gametocyte stage, F-actin forms a dynamic and extensive network that passes through the whole cell and is enriched at the tips of the parasite.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Hliscs et al., 2015.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy revealed a complex F-actin network in P. falciparum parasites.
source: For better visualisation of F-actin structures, we used super-resolution microscopy (SR-SIM) which revealed a complex F-actin network in these parasites (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite.
source: Interestingly, F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2 lower left panel), which is also the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The FV is at the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
source: Interestingly, F-actin was prominent around the FV of the parasite (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2 lower left panel), which is also the basal end of the newly-formed daughter parasites during the final stages of cytokinesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: When the actin-chromobody-labelled network was co-stained with an antibody raised against parasite actin, similar structures as seen with chromobody were apparent.
source: When we co-stained the actin-chromobody-labelled network with an antibody raised against parasite actin (Angrisano et al., 2012), similar structures as seen with chromobody were apparent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Angrisano et al., 2012.

claim: The staining of chromobody and actin antibody was not identical, perhaps due to the masking of antibody binding sites by other binding proteins.
source: The staining was however not identical perhaps due to the masking of antibody binding sites by other binding proteins, which was also observed previously for T. gondii actin (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.6 was obtained for co-localisation of the CB-EME signal with that of the actin-antibody.
source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the CB-EME signal with that of the actin-antibody, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.6, in comparison to R values of 0.2 when the CBEME signal was tested for co-localisation with the DAPI signal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claim: IMC markers GAP45 and MTIP showed normal staining in CB-EME expressing parasites.
source: IMC markers GAP45 and MTIP showed normal staining in CB-EME expressing parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of chromobodies does not cause significant phenotypic effects and allows reliable labelling of the F-actin cytoskeleton.
source: Together, our data show that expression of chromobodies does not cause significant phenotypic effects and allow reliable labelling of the F-actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Upon disruption of PfACT1, CB-EME and CB-HALO labelled F-actin structures completely disappeared in late trophozoites and schizonts.
source: Upon induction with RAP in 1h-old ring stages, CB-EME (Figure 2, Video 7) and CB-HALO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) labelled F-actin structures completely disappeared in late trophozoites and schizonts and closely resembled parasites treated with cytochalasin-D (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: PfACT1-disrupted parasites could not invade new erythrocytes.
source: As previously reported (Das et al., 2017), PfACT1-disrupted parasites could not invade new erythrocytes (Figure 2B(ii)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B(ii) and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: A ≈ 10x reduction in emerald signal was observed upon disruption of PfACT1.
source: We observed a ≈ 10x reduction in emerald signal upon disruption of PfACT1 (Figure 2C), which could be due to the proteasomal degradation of actin-chromobodies, when they are not bound to actin, as was seen by others for a different chromobody (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Tang et al., 2016.

claim: Apicoplast inheritance depends on PfACT1.
source: We previously reported that apicoplast inheritance depends on PfACT1 (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: Apicoplasts are in close proximity with F-actin structures.
source: In order to determine the localisation of F-actin during apicoplast segregation we used deconvolution microscopy on fixed parasites stained with the apicoplast marker CPN60, which revealed apicoplasts to be in close proximity with F-actin structures (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.4 was obtained for colocalisation of the apicoplast(s) signal with the CB-EME channel.
source: A Pearson's R value of 0.4 was obtained for colocalisation of the apicoplast(s) signal with the CB-EME channel in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B lower panel, as compared to 0.1 with the DAPI channel.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claim: 75% ± 7% of apicoplasts lie apposed to the F-actin network.
source: We also scored for individual apicoplast signals which are proximal to the F-actin network (example shown in Figure 2E) and found 75% ± 7% apicoplasts to lie apposed to the F-actin network (N = 445).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: Upon disruption of PfACT1, a defect in apicoplast segregation was apparent.
source: Upon disruption of PfACT1, a defect in apicoplast segregation was apparent (Figure 2D PfAct1cKO), which recapitulated the phenotype previously observed (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: No obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites.
source: In contrast, no obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7) as previously reported (Das et al., 2017), implying that unlike apicoplasts, mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7, and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: Mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
source: In contrast, no obvious defects in mitochondria segregation could be detected in PfACT1-disrupted parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 7) as previously reported (Das et al., 2017), implying that unlike apicoplasts, mitochondria do not require F-actin for migration into daughter cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of mitochondrial segregation defects in PfACT1-disrupted parasites.

claim: Stable time-averaged F-actin peaks were observed, which could be easily distinguished from background and from the signal in PfACT1KO parasites.
source: Stable time-averaged F-actin peaks were observed, which could be easily distinguished from background and from the signal in PfACT1KO parasites (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The highest time-averaged intensity peaks were observed around the food vacuole.
source: We observed the highest time-averaged intensity peaks around the food vacuole, as also noted by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, lower left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction.
source: Previously, PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction and PfFRM2 to the cytosol (Baum et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: PfFRM2 has been localised to the cytosol.
source: Previously, PfFRM1 has been localised to the invasion junction and PfFRM2 to the cytosol (Baum et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: Formin-2 is the main nucleator of F-actin during intracellular parasite development.
source: Since we observed the intracellular F-actin network in the cytosol, we speculated that Formin-2 is the main nucleator of F-actin during intracellular parasite development.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed localisation of F-actin and Formin-2.

claim: Formins possess a formin homology (FH) one and an FH2 domain, which nucleate actin monomers as well as elongate unbranched F-actin by continuous processive binding to the barbed end of the filament.
source: Formins possess a formin homology (FH) one and an FH2 domain, which nucleate actin monomers as well as elongate unbranched F-actin by continuous processive binding to the barbed end of the filament (Courtemanche, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Courtemanche, 2018.

claim: In a previous report, only FH1/FH2 domains were described for apicomplexan formins.
source: In a previous report (Baum et al., 2008b), only FH1/FH2 domains were described for apicomplexan formins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: Tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains were found in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1.
source: Here, we queried for presence of known PFAM domains using NCBI conserved domain search and in addition to FH1/FH2, found tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1, while a PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2.
source: Here, we queried for presence of known PFAM domains using NCBI conserved domain search and in addition to FH1/FH2, found tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domains in both PfFRM1 and TgFRM1, while a PTEN C2-like domain was recognised in PfFRM2 and TgFRM2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Formin-1 and Formin-2 with different N-terminal domains diverged early in evolution and different domain organisations have been retained for different functions.
source: This led us to hypothesise that Formin-1 and Formin-2 with different N-terminal domains diverged early in evolution and different domain organisations have been retained for different functions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the bioinformatic findings.

claim: Formin-2-like sequences are found in a different clade from Formin-1-like sequences.
source: We queried for FH2-domain containing proteins from various apicomplexans and found that Formin-2-like sequences are found in a different clade from Formin-1-like sequences (Figure 3B), as also previously noted (Baum et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3B and citation to Baum et al., 2008b.

claim: The PTEN-C2-domain (or a diverged PTEN-C2 domain) was found only in Formin-2-like sequences.
source: Strikingly, the PTEN-C2-domain (or a diverged PTEN-C2 domain) was found only in Formin-2-like sequences (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment.
source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Das et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: A class II rice Formin uses the PTEN-C2 domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes.
source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: A similar mechanism to rice Formin operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
source: Interestingly, PTEN-C2 domains are important for membrane recruitment (Das et al., 2003) and a class II rice Formin uses this domain to be recruited to chloroplast membranes (Zhang et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesise that a similar mechanism operates for apicoplast recruitment of Formin-2 sequences in apicomplexans.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity of PTEN-C2 domains in rice Formin and apicomplexan Formin-2.

claim: TgFRM2 was found to be localised adjacent to apicoplast(s).
source: Upon co-staining with the anti-apicoplast antibody G2-Trx (Biddau and Sheiner, unpublished), we found TgFRM2 to be localised adjacent to apicoplast(s) (Figure 3E), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: 30% of apicoplasts partially colocalised and 58% apicoplasts were adjacent to and in contact with the TgFRM2 signal.
source: Upon quantification of co-localisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found 30% apicoplasts partially colocalised and 58% apicoplasts adjacent to and in contact with the TgFRM2 signal (n = 142).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PfFRM2 showed a punctate pattern within cells.
source: PfFRM2 showed a punctate pattern within cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: PfFRM2 localises in close proximity to apicoplasts throughout the 48 hr Plasmodium blood stage life-cycle.
source: Next, we checked for PfFRM2 localisation in relation to apicoplasts and observed a close proximity of the apicoplasts with most of the PfFRM2 punctae throughout the 48 hr Plasmodium blood stage life-cycle (Figure 3J), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and 3K.

claim: A Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 was obtained for co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae.
source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 (N = 4), the high variance implying that the close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-localisation analysis.

claim: The close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
source: Upon quantification of co-localisation of the apicoplast signal with that of the formin punctae, we obtained a Pearson's R value of 0.55 ± 0.2 (N = 4), the high variance implying that the close proximity of the apicoplasts to Formin-2 may be dynamic.
evidence: This is inferred from the high variance in the Pearson's R value.

claim: Excision of the pffrm2 locus was confirmed by diagnostic PCR.
source: Excision was determined by diagnostic PCR of the genomic locus (Figure 4B) and fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) was measured by a growth curve which showed significant loss of viability (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) showed significant loss of viability.
source: Excision was determined by diagnostic PCR of the genomic locus (Figure 4B) and fitness of the PfFRM2 conditional knock out (cKO) was measured by a growth curve which showed significant loss of viability (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of PfFRM2 protein was ~90% as determined by Western blot.
source: Loss of protein was ~90% (averaged from three independent experiments) as determined by Western blot (Figure 4D) and was confirmed by IFA (Figure 4E), which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites (N = 350).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Loss of PfFRM2 protein was confirmed by IFA, which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites.
source: Loss of protein was ~90% (averaged from three independent experiments) as determined by Western blot (Figure 4D) and was confirmed by IFA (Figure 4E), which indicated a loss of protein in ~95% parasites (N = 350).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Giemsa stained PfFRM2 cKO parasites were dysmorphic with apparent inclusions of haemoglobin.
source: Giemsa stained PfFRM2 cKO parasites were dysmorphic with apparent inclusions of haemoglobin (Figure 4F, red arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of parasites with normally segregated apicoplasts was significantly reduced in PfFRM2 cKO parasites, with a high percentage of cells showing collapsed or morphologically aberrant apicoplasts.
source: The number of parasites with normally segregated apicoplasts was significantly reduced, with a high percentage of cells showing collapsed or morphologically aberrant apicoplasts (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: A range of apicoplast phenotypes was evident in PfFRM2 cKO parasites, from totally collapsed, intermediate to apparently normal.
source: A range of apicoplast phenotypes was evident, from totally collapsed, intermediate to apparently normal (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) did not improve viability of PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
source: To determine if the loss of viability of the PfFRM2 cKO parasites was solely due to loss of the apicoplast, we attempted to rescue the phenotype with 200 µM isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) which has been previously shown to complement growth in parasites lacking apicoplasts (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011). However, we did not see any improvement in viability (Figure 4I), indicating that the loss of fitness is due to additional defects caused by abrogation of F-actin dynamics in the parasite, which we shall address shortly in Section 5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and citation to Yeh and DeRisi, 2011.

claim: The loss of fitness in PfFRM2 cKO parasites is due to additional defects caused by abrogation of F-actin dynamics in the parasite.
source: To determine if the loss of viability of the PfFRM2 cKO parasites was solely due to loss of the apicoplast, we attempted to rescue the phenotype with 200 µM isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) which has been previously shown to complement growth in parasites lacking apicoplasts (Yeh and DeRisi, 2011). However, we did not see any improvement in viability (Figure 4I), indicating that the loss of fitness is due to additional defects caused by abrogation of F-actin dynamics in the parasite, which we shall address shortly in Section 5.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of IPP to rescue the phenotype.

claim: A complete abrogation of the dynamic F-actin network was observed in mature schizont stage parasites upon DiCre-mediated excision of PfFRM2 in ring stages.
source: Upon DiCre-mediated excision in ring stages, we saw a complete abrogation of the dynamic F-actin network in mature schizont stage parasites (Figure 5B RAP), which dropped from exhibiting an F-actin network in 92 ± 5% cells in WT to 5 ± 4% cells in PfFRM2 cKO (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: F-actin network dropped from exhibiting in 92 ± 5% cells in WT to 5 ± 4% cells in PfFRM2 cKO.
source: Upon DiCre-mediated excision in ring stages, we saw a complete abrogation of the dynamic F-actin network in mature schizont stage parasites (Figure 5B RAP), which dropped from exhibiting an F-actin network in 92 ± 5% cells in WT to 5 ± 4% cells in PfFRM2 cKO (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: Surface intensity plots showed a dramatic reduction in F-actin peaks in the PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
source: Surface intensity plots showed a dramatic reduction in F-actin peaks in the PfFRM2 cKO parasites (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The apicoplast inheritance phenotype was confirmed in PfFRM2 cKO parasites expressing CB-EME.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the apicoplast inheritance phenotype in PfFRM2 cKO parasites expressing CB-EME (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: PfFRM2 punctae localised primarily with CB-EME-labelled filamentous structures.
source: IFA analysis showed PfFRM2 punctae localised primarily with CB-EME-labelled filamentous structures (Pearson's R value = 0.36, as compared to 0.02 with the DAPI channel) (Figure 5B, DMSO and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 80% ± 6% of individual PfFRM2-HA punctae were found closely apposed to the F-actin signal.
source: When we manually counted the individual PfFRM2-HA punctae, we found 80% ± 6% closely apposed to the F-actin signal (N = 200).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of nuclei was observed in PfFRM2 cKO parasites 40 hr post RAP-treatment, as compared to the DMSO control.
source: As a first step towards characterisation of additional defects, we determined the number of nuclei in PfFRM2 cKO parasites 40 hr post RAP-treatment, and found a significant decrease in the number of nuclei in these parasites, as compared to the DMSO control (Figure 6A), indicating a defect in development or schizogony.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A defect in development or schizogony was indicated in PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
source: As a first step towards characterisation of additional defects, we determined the number of nuclei in PfFRM2 cKO parasites 40 hr post RAP-treatment, and found a significant decrease in the number of nuclei in these parasites, as compared to the DMSO control (Figure 6A), indicating a defect in development or schizogony.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant decrease in the number of nuclei.

claim: PfACT1 is required for normal cytokinesis.
source: Since PfACT1 is required for normal cytokinesis (Das et al., 2017), we examined if the IMC is normally formed in PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: Fully segmented IMC staining dropped from 58 ± 8% in WT to 19 ± 8% in PfFRM2 cKOs.
source: Fully segmented IMC staining dropped from 58 ± 8% in WT to 19 ± 8% in PfFRM2 cKOs (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Conjoined merozoites were found in PfFRM2 cKOs after egress.
source: When we allowed these Percoll-purified mature PfFRM2 cKO parasites to egress and compared them to control parasites, we found conjoined merozoites in PfFRM2 cKOs (Figure 6D,E), a defect previously seen in PfACT1 cKO parasites (Das et al., 2017), indicating that PfFRM2 and PfACT1 coordinate cytokinesis in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and 6E, and citation to Das et al., 2017.

claim: PfFRM2 and PfACT1 coordinate cytokinesis in P. falciparum.
source: When we allowed these Percoll-purified mature PfFRM2 cKO parasites to egress and compared them to control parasites, we found conjoined merozoites in PfFRM2 cKOs (Figure 6D,E), a defect previously seen in PfACT1 cKO parasites (Das et al., 2017), indicating that PfFRM2 and PfACT1 coordinate cytokinesis in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar cytokinesis defects in PfFRM2 and PfACT1 cKO parasites.

claim: The ability of F-actin polymerisation at the parasite apex was not compromised in PfFRM2 cKO parasites.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that the ability of F-actin polymerisation at the parasite apex was not compromised in PfFRM2 cKO parasites (Figure 6F), strongly indicating distinct functions of PfFRM1 and PfFRM2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PfFRM1 and PfFRM2 have distinct functions.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that the ability of F-actin polymerisation at the parasite apex was not compromised in PfFRM2 cKO parasites (Figure 6F), strongly indicating distinct functions of PfFRM1 and PfFRM2.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of PfFRM2 cKO parasites to polymerise F-actin at the apex.

claim: PfFRM2 cKO parasites did reinvade RBCs and established ring stage parasites despite showing a significant growth defect.
source: Despite showing a significant growth defect, PfFRM2 cKO parasites did reinvade RBCs and established ring stage parasites.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: No F-actin dynamics could be observed in early trophozoite stage PfFRM2 cKO parasites or peripheral accumulations of F-actin in these parasites.
source: In good agreement with the observations above and a general role of PfFRM2 in F-actin nucleation during intracellular parasite development, we could not observe any F-actin dynamics in early trophozoite stage parasites or peripheral accumulations of F-actin in these parasites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TgFRM2-HA formed punctae on the CB-EME labelled F-actin network within the parasite.
source: Similar to P. falciparum, TgFRM2-HA formed punctae on the CB-EME labelled F-actin network within the parasite. There it appeared to co-localise with a polymerisation centre (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Tg), recently also described in an independent report (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: TgFRM2-HA appeared to co-localise with a polymerisation centre.
source: Similar to P. falciparum, TgFRM2-HA formed punctae on the CB-EME labelled F-actin network within the parasite. There it appeared to co-localise with a polymerisation centre (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Tg), recently also described in an independent report (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Excision of the tgfrm2 locus upon RAP-treatment was confirmed by diagnostic PCR.
source: Integration of the C-terminal YFP-tag and LoxP sites was confirmed by diagnostic PCR, as was excision of the tgfrm2 locus upon RAP-treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Excision of TgFRM2 was apparent in 36 ± 4% of vacuoles, as assessed by quantification of parasites where no TgFRM2 could be detected by IFA.
source: Upon RAP-treatment, excision of TgFRM2 was apparent in 36 ± 4% (n = 300) of vacuoles, as assessed by quantification of parasites where no TgFRM2 could be detected by IFA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: Loss of TgFRM2 staining correlated with an apicoplast segregation phenotype in 65 ± 7% of parasites.
source: Importantly, loss of TgFRM2 staining correlated with an apicoplast segregation phenotype in 65 ± 7% (n = 300) of parasites (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A baseline apicoplast segregation phenotype was observed in 1% (±0; n = 300) of vacuoles in the control population.
source: A baseline apicoplast segregation phenotype was observed in 1% (±0; n = 300) of vacuoles in the control population.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: Loss of TgFRM2 had no impact on mitochondrial replication or morphology.
source: Loss of TgFRM2 had no impact on mitochondrial replication or morphology (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Intracellular F-actin formed a polymerisation centre adjacent to the apicoplast in T. gondii.
source: Transient expression of CB-EME in LoxPTgFRM2 parasites enabled us to image F-actin and demonstrated that, in good agreement with data from P. falciparum, intracellular F-actin formed a polymerisation centre adjacent to the apicoplast (Figure 7C control).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Excision of TgFRM2 led to the disappearance of intracellular F-actin at the polymerisation centre.
source: Intriguingly, excision of TgFRM2 (Figure 7C RAP) led to the disappearance of intracellular F-actin at the polymerisation centre, while (in contrast to P. falciparum), the intra-vacuolar F-actin network was still present (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The intra-vacuolar F-actin network was still present in TgFRM2 cKO parasites, in contrast to P. falciparum.
source: Intriguingly, excision of TgFRM2 (Figure 7C RAP) led to the disappearance of intracellular F-actin at the polymerisation centre, while (in contrast to P. falciparum), the intra-vacuolar F-actin network was still present (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In Toxoplasma, actin polymerisation within the residual body (and consequently the formation of the intra-vacuolar F-actin network) has been attributed to Formin-3.
source: In Toxoplasma, actin polymerisation within the residual body (and consequently the formation of the intra-vacuolar F-actin network) has been attributed to Formin-3 (Tosetti et al., 2019), which is absent in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Formin-3 is absent in P. falciparum.
source: In Toxoplasma, actin polymerisation within the residual body (and consequently the formation of the intra-vacuolar F-actin network) has been attributed to Formin-3 (Tosetti et al., 2019), which is absent in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between the two parasites.

claim: In wild-type T. gondii parasites, the highest CB-EME intensities were observed at the apical and posterior poles and anterior to the nucleus.
source: In wild-type parasites, the highest CB-EME intensities were observed at the apical and posterior poles and anterior to the nucleus (Figure 8A, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Video 9.

claim: Skeletonisation analysis on videos of wild-type T. gondii parasites showed actin accumulation in the periphery of intracellular parasites.
source: Additionally, skeletonisation analysis on videos of wild-type parasites showed actin accumulation in the periphery of intracellular parasites (Figure 8B, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Video 9.

claim: Live imaging revealed that the actin polymerisation centre anterior to the nucleus is highly dynamic and frequently interacts with peripheral actin in T. gondii.
source: Live imaging further revealed that the actin polymerisation centre anterior to the nucleus is highly dynamic and frequently interacts with peripheral actin (Figure 8C, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and Video 9.

claim: Disrupting tgfrm2 using the conditional CRISPR/CAS9 system resulted in loss of F-actin at the nucleation centre anterior to the nucleus.
source: In agreement with observations made using the DiCre-system (Figure 7C), disrupting tgfrm2 using the conditional CRISPR/CAS9 system also resulted in loss of F-actin at the nucleation centre anterior to the nucleus (Figure 8A right panel, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Video 9.

claim: The abundance of peripheral actin was strongly reduced in TgFRM2-cKO parasites.
source: Interestingly, the abundance of peripheral actin was also strongly reduced in TgFRM2-cKO parasites (Figure 8B, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Video 9.

claim: The TgFRM2-mediated actin polymerisation centre anterior to the nucleus contributes to the parasite peripheral actin pool.
source: Consequently, it is conceivable that the TgFRM2-mediated actin polymerisation centre anterior to the nucleus contributes to the parasite peripheral actin pool, making Formin-2 a key player in regulating actin distribution within intracellular parasites.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in peripheral actin upon loss of TgFRM2.

claim: Formin-2 is a key player in regulating actin distribution within intracellular parasites.
source: Consequently, it is conceivable that the TgFRM2-mediated actin polymerisation centre anterior to the nucleus contributes to the parasite peripheral actin pool, making Formin-2 a key player in regulating actin distribution within intracellular parasites.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of TgFRM2 in maintaining the actin polymerisation centre and peripheral actin.

claim: F-actin was still measurable and visible at the apical and the basal poles, as well as in the residual body of TgFRM2-cKO parasites.
source: Intriguingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, F-actin was still measurable and visible at the apical and the basal poles, as well as in the residual body of TgFRM2-cKO parasites.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: At the apical and basal poles and in the residual body, actin polymerisation is probably mediated by the nucleation factors TgFRM1 and TgFRM3.
source: At these locations, actin polymerisation is probably mediated by the nucleation factors TgFRM1 and TgFRM3 which a recent study (Tosetti et al., 2019) localised to the apical tip and the residual body, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Tosetti and colleagues proposed peripheral actin flux towards the basal end of extracellular parasites.
source: Tosetti and colleagues proposed peripheral actin flux towards the basal end of extracellular parasites (Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Kymographs of wild-type T. gondii parasites showed trajectories representing CB-EME particle movement towards the apical and basal poles, indicating bi-directional actin flow all along the lateral parasite axis.
source: Kymographs of wild-type parasites showed trajectories representing CB-EME particle movement towards the apical and basal poles (red signal represents forward displacement, while green signal represents backward displacement on kymographs, Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2; Videos 9, 10, 11 and 12), indicating bi-directional actin flow all along the lateral parasite axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: In TgAct cKO parasites, no distinguishable tracks could be identified by kymograph analysis, when compared to background noise.
source: In TgAct cKO parasites, no distinguishable tracks could be identified by kymograph analysis, when compared to background noise (Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2B, Video 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2B, and Video 10.

claim: TgADF cKO kymographs represent the previously described phenotype of strong static actin accumulation at the basal end of the parasite with no obvious F-actin dynamics at the periphery.
source: TgADF cKO kymographs represent the previously described phenotype of strong static actin accumulation at the basal end of the parasite with no obvious F-actin dynamics at the periphery (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D, blue signal on kymographs, Video 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D and Video 11.

claim: Kymographs of TgFRM2 cKO parasites appear more diffuse, although some tracks could still be observed.
source: Kymographs of TgFRM2 cKO parasites appear more diffuse, although some tracks could still be observed (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, and Video 9.
